prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When daylighting into a building interior, this daylighting structure attenuates the brightness of a setting sun or a winter-time incoming light of small elevation angles, and causes the incoming light to be diffusely emitted toward the ceiling surface or into a deep portion of the indoor space domain regardless of the elevation angle thereof. An incoming light (E20) of 20° in elevation angle is caused to be diffusely emitted toward the ceiling surface on the internal upper side of the building through the refraction and reflection actions mediated by a light-transmitting material mounted in a horizontal direction opening of a wall. The light-transmitting material comprises: an outdoor region curved surface wherethrough the incoming light is refracted and let into the interior of the light-transmitting material in a focused form; a lower side reflection surface internally reflecting the refracted incoming light; and an indoor region curved surface wherefrom the internally reflected light is refracted and emitted toward the ceiling surface in a diffused form. Also disclosed are the installation wherein the light-transmitting material is inclined from the illustrated horizontal state, and the installation of a plurality of the light-transmitting materials, each in upper and lower directions and left and right directions.

outputs.L1: When used to introduce daylight into a building interior, this daylighting structure attenuates the brightness of a setting sun or winter sunlight entering at low elevation angles, and diffusely emits the incoming light toward the ceiling surface or into a deep portion of the indoor space, regardless of the light’s elevation angle. Incoming light (E20) having an elevation angle of 20° is diffusely emitted toward the ceiling surface on the upper interior side of the building through refraction and reflection mediated by a light-transmitting material mounted in a horizontal opening in a wall. The light-transmitting material comprises: an outdoor-region curved surface through which the incoming light is refracted and introduced into the interior of the light-transmitting material in a focused form; a lower-side reflection surface that internally reflects the refracted incoming light; and an indoor-region curved surface from which the internally reflected light is refracted and emitted toward the ceiling surface in a diffused form. Also disclosed are an installation in which the light-transmitting material is inclined from the illustrated horizontal state, and an installation comprising a plurality of such light-transmitting materials arranged in the upper and lower directions and in the left and right directions.
outputs.L2:
This daylighting device reduces the intensity of low-angle sunlight entering a building, such as evening sunlight or winter light, and redirects it so that it is diffusely projected toward the ceiling or farther into the interior space, regardless of the light’s elevation angle.

For example, incoming light (E20) at an elevation angle of 20° is guided toward the upper interior ceiling surface by refraction and reflection through a light-transmitting member installed in a horizontally oriented opening in a wall. The light-transmitting member includes an outdoor-side curved surface that refracts the incoming light and introduces it into the member in a concentrated manner; a lower reflective surface that internally reflects the refracted light; and an indoor-side curved surface that refracts the internally reflected light and emits it in a diffused state toward the ceiling.

The disclosure also includes arrangements in which the light-transmitting member is installed at an inclination relative to the illustrated horizontal position, as well as configurations using multiple light-transmitting members arranged vertically and horizontally.
outputs.L3:
The daylighting structure is designed to improve indoor lighting conditions by controlling and redirecting incoming natural light. In particular, it reduces the brightness and glare of low-elevation sunlight, such as light from the setting sun or winter sunlight, which can otherwise enter a room at a shallow angle and cause discomfort.

At the same time, the structure efficiently uses incoming daylight by diffusely emitting it toward the ceiling or directing it deep into the indoor space, regardless of the elevation angle of the incoming light. This helps create a more uniform and comfortable indoor illumination environment while reducing excessive brightness near windows.

For example, when incoming light at an elevation angle of approximately 20° enters a horizontally mounted light-transmitting material, the light is refracted by an outdoor curved refracting surface and then reflected by a lower internal reflection surface. The redirected light subsequently exits through an indoor curved surface as diffused light, illuminating the upper portion of the interior space, particularly the ceiling area.

The light-transmitting material is therefore formed with multiple optical surfaces that cooperate to control the path of sunlight. These include an outdoor curved refracting surface for receiving and refracting external light, a lower internal reflection surface for reflecting the refracted light upward or inward, and an indoor curved surface for emitting the light in a diffused manner into the room.

The daylighting system may be installed in a horizontal configuration, but it is not limited to such an arrangement. It can also be installed in an inclined orientation depending on the building design, window shape, or desired lighting direction. In addition, multiple units of the structure may be arranged vertically and horizontally to cover a larger window area or to provide more extensive daylight control across an indoor space.
outputs.L4:
A daylighting structure is designed to improve the use of natural sunlight entering a building through a wall opening, particularly when the sunlight arrives at a low elevation angle, such as during sunrise, sunset, or the winter season. The structure includes a light-transmitting member installed in an opening formed in a wall, window area, clerestory, or similar portion of a building envelope. This light-transmitting member is made of glass, resin, acrylic, polycarbonate, or another transparent or translucent material, and is shaped so that incident sunlight is optically controlled as it passes through the structure.

Unlike an ordinary flat window, the daylighting structure has a specially formed cross-sectional shape, surface profile, or internal optical geometry. When low-angle sunlight strikes the structure, the light is refracted at the incident surface, guided within the material by internal reflection, and then emitted from another surface in a redirected and diffused form. As a result, sunlight that would otherwise enter the room at a shallow angle and cause glare, excessive brightness near the window, or uncomfortable direct exposure is redirected upward toward the ceiling or farther into the interior space.

The ceiling and upper wall surfaces then act as secondary reflecting surfaces, scattering the light more evenly throughout the room. This helps brighten areas that are located away from the window and reduces the sharp contrast between the region near the opening and the deeper indoor region. In this way, the daylighting structure improves the overall distribution of daylight without relying solely on artificial lighting.

The structure is particularly effective for sunlight having a low solar altitude. During winter, when the sun remains low in the sky for much of the day, the device can capture and redirect sunlight that would otherwise penetrate directly and create glare. Similarly, in the morning or evening, when sunlight enters at a shallow angle, the structure can guide the incoming rays toward useful interior surfaces rather than allowing them to shine directly into occupants’ eyes or onto work surfaces.

The optical shape of the light-transmitting material may include curved surfaces, prism-like portions, wedge-shaped sections, serrated surfaces, lenses, or internal reflection faces. These features may be arranged so that light entering from different elevation angles is still redirected in a generally upward or inward direction. Therefore, even when the sun’s position changes throughout the day or across seasons, the daylighting structure can maintain a useful daylighting effect.

Because the emitted light is diffused or spread over a wider area, the structure reduces uncomfortable glare and localized hot spots. At the same time, it increases the amount of usable natural light reaching the interior of the building. This can improve visual comfort, reduce dependence on electric lighting during daytime hours, and contribute to energy savings.

The daylighting structure may be incorporated into new construction or retrofitted into existing wall openings. It may be used in residential buildings, offices, schools, factories, public facilities, or other spaces where improved daylight distribution is desired. By combining refraction, internal reflection, and diffusion in a single light-transmitting element, the structure provides a passive and efficient way to capture low-elevation sunlight and deliver it to the ceiling or deeper indoor areas, thereby creating a brighter, more comfortable interior environment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract describing a daylighting structure installed in a horizontal wall opening that redirects low-elevation sunlight toward the ceiling using a curved transparent material, refraction, internal reflection, and diffuse emission.
counterfactuals.output: A daylighting structure is configured for installation in a substantially horizontal wall opening, such as a roof or skylight aperture, to introduce and redistribute exterior sunlight within an interior space. The structure includes a curved body formed of transparent or translucent optical material having an exterior light-receiving surface and an interior light-emitting surface. Low-elevation incident sunlight entering the curved body is refracted at the exterior surface and guided through the body by refraction and internal reflection along one or more curved optical paths. The guided light is redirected upwardly or laterally toward an interior ceiling surface rather than being transmitted primarily downward. At least a portion of the interior surface, or an associated diffuser, is configured to diffusely emit the redirected light into the room, thereby producing indirect daylight illumination and reducing glare, localized solar penetration, and excessive contrast. The daylighting structure may be formed as a unitary curved glazing element or as an insert mountable within a conventional horizontal opening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the invention shown in a patent figure: incoming light at a 20° elevation angle enters a light-transmitting member, is focused by an outdoor curved surface, reflected by a lower internal surface, and emitted diffusely from an indoor curved surface toward the ceiling.
counterfactuals.output: The invention is a daylighting device that guides sunlight indoors. Incoming light enters a transparent light-transmitting member at a relatively low elevation angle, such as 20°. An outdoor-facing curved surface refracts and focuses the light inside the member, where it is reflected by a lower internal reflective surface. The light is then directed to an indoor-facing curved surface, which emits the light diffusely upward toward the ceiling. This spreads natural light into the room indirectly, reducing glare while improving interior illumination.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical description of a building daylighting device that attenuates glare from setting sun or winter sunlight and sends low-angle incoming light deep indoors, including variants with inclined installation and multiple units arranged vertically and horizontally.
counterfactuals.output:
A building daylighting device is provided for admitting low-angle sunlight into an interior space while reducing direct glare associated with setting sun, winter sun, or other low solar-elevation conditions. The device may be installed at or adjacent to a window, clerestory, glazed façade, light well, or other daylight aperture, and is configured to intercept incident sunlight arriving at a shallow elevation angle and redirect at least a portion of that light upwardly and/or inwardly toward the ceiling or deeper portions of the room.

The device includes one or more optical elements having an incident-light receiving side and an interior-light emitting side. Each optical element may comprise a reflective, refractive, diffusive, or hybrid optical body shaped to change the propagation direction of incoming sunlight. In one implementation, the element includes an upper glare-shielding surface and a lower light-redirecting surface. The glare-shielding surface blocks, absorbs, scatters, or reflects a direct line of sight to the low sun, thereby attenuating discomfort glare for occupants. The light-redirecting surface receives sunlight from below or from a low incident angle and redirects the light toward an upper interior region, such as a ceiling plane, from which the light may be secondarily reflected to provide diffuse illumination deeper in the space.

The optical element may be formed as a louver, prism, wedge, curved reflector, compound parabolic reflector, faceted reflector, microprismatic plate, translucent refractive blade, or a combination thereof. The element may have a specular, semi-specular, matte, or selectively diffusing surface finish depending on the desired balance between light throw distance and glare control. Reflective surfaces may be formed from polished metal, metallized polymer, coated glass, high-reflectance laminate, or molded plastic with reflective coating. Refractive or prismatic portions may be formed from glass, acrylic, polycarbonate, or other transparent or translucent material.

In operation, sunlight entering at a low angle from the exterior is intercepted by the device before reaching the normal occupant field of view. A first portion of the light is redirected upwardly toward the ceiling or toward a high interior wall region. A second portion may be diffused to reduce luminance contrast. A third portion may be rejected outwardly or absorbed to prevent excessive brightness, solar heat gain, or direct glare. The geometry of the device is selected so that sunlight at lower solar elevations is admitted and redirected, while light above a selected cutoff angle may pass, be partially shaded, or be redirected differently.

The device may be installed in a generally horizontal orientation, for example as a shelf-like member extending inwardly or outwardly from a window opening. In another variant, the device is installed at an inclined angle relative to the horizontal or relative to the glazing plane. Inclined installation allows the optical surfaces to be tuned to particular solar altitude ranges, façade orientations, room depths, or occupant viewing positions. For example, the device may be tilted upward toward the interior to increase ceiling illumination, tilted downward toward the exterior to increase low-angle solar interception, or inclined in both vertical and lateral directions to account for oblique sunlight from the west, southwest, east, or southeast.

Multiple devices may be arranged vertically within a window or façade opening. In this configuration, the units may function as a daylighting louver array. Each vertically spaced unit intercepts a corresponding band of incoming low-angle sunlight and redirects it inwardly and upwardly, while the spacing between units may permit exterior view, ventilation, or additional daylight admission. The pitch, tilt angle, curvature, surface finish, and optical cutoff angle of the upper units may differ from those of the lower units to compensate for different incident angles and occupant sightlines. Lower units may provide stronger glare shielding, while upper units may be optimized for deeper light penetration.

Multiple devices may also be arranged horizontally across a glazing system. Horizontally adjacent units may be repeated along the width of a window, curtain wall, skylight, or clerestory. The units may have identical optical geometry or may be individually tuned according to their position, façade orientation, expected solar azimuth, or room layout. For example, units near the side of a window may include lateral redirecting facets that steer light toward the center of the room, while central units may redirect light primarily upward and inward.

In a further variant, the devices are arranged in both vertical and horizontal arrays, forming a grid or matrix of glare-attenuating daylighting modules. Such a modular configuration may be integrated into an insulating glass unit, mounted on the interior side of glazing, mounted on the exterior side as a shading and daylighting assembly, or suspended within a double-skin façade cavity. The modules may be fixed, manually adjustable, or motorized. Adjustable versions may change inclination, spacing, or surface exposure in response to sun position, time of day, season, sky condition, interior illuminance, or occupant preference.

The device may include side shields, end caps, baffles, secondary reflectors, or diffusing films to suppress stray light and prevent high-luminance images of the sun from being visible to occupants. The upper or leading edge of each element may be shaped to create a cutoff angle below which direct sunlight is intercepted and above which diffuse skylight or selected daylight components may enter. The lower surface may include a concave, convex, or multi-faceted profile that spreads redirected light over a broad ceiling area rather than concentrating it into a bright spot.

The daylighting device is particularly suitable for façades exposed to low solar altitude, such as west-facing façades in the late afternoon, east-facing façades in the morning, and south-facing façades during winter in the northern hemisphere. By attenuating direct glare while redirecting useful low-angle sunlight deeper into the room, the device improves visual comfort, reduces reliance on electric lighting, and can increase the effective daylight penetration distance of the building aperture.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an abstract for a daylight control window element comprising an outdoor curved refracting surface, a lower reflection surface, and an indoor curved emitting surface, explaining how it redirects E20 incoming light toward an interior ceiling.
counterfactuals.output: An architectural daylight control window element is configured to redirect incident daylight from a low solar elevation into a room toward an interior ceiling surface. The element includes an outdoor-facing curved refracting surface arranged to receive incoming light, including light incident at approximately E20, and to refract the received light into the body of the element. A lower reflection surface is positioned to intercept the refracted light and reflect it upwardly and inwardly. An indoor-facing curved emitting surface then transmits the reflected light into the interior space while further refracting the light so that it exits in a direction aimed generally toward the ceiling rather than toward an occupant’s direct field of view. By combining refraction at the outdoor curved surface, reflection at the lower surface, and controlled emission through the indoor curved surface, the window element improves daylight penetration, promotes ceiling illumination, and reduces glare from low-angle sunlight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Translate or rewrite in English a Japanese patent abstract about a light-transmitting material mounted in a horizontal opening of a wall, designed to refract, internally reflect, and diffuse low-angle daylight into a room.
counterfactuals.output: A light-transmitting member is installed in a horizontal opening formed in a wall to introduce daylight into a room. The member is designed so that incident sunlight, particularly low-angle daylight entering from outside, is refracted upon entry, guided by internal reflection, and then emitted into the interior in a diffused state. By controlling refraction, total internal reflection, and diffusion within the material, daylight can be directed deeper into the room while reducing glare and uneven illumination. This structure enables effective use of natural light even when the sun is at a low elevation, improving indoor brightness and lighting comfort without relying solely on artificial lighting.
